sentence: All eight billion, with room to breathe.
claim: About 8.2 billion people were alive in mid-2024.
source_title: World Population Prospects 2024 (UN DESA Population Division); news.un.org/en/story/2024/07/1151971
note: Said as 'eight billion' (the spine shows 8.2 billion).

sentence: So give each person half a square meter, the room a calm crowd keeps.
claim: A crowd moves comfortably below about 2 people per square metre, i.e. about half a square metre each.
source_title: Crowd-density thresholds (ScienceAlert; also Waseda University WIAS and NPR on crowd safety), summarising Fruin's levels of service and G. K. Still's crowd science
note: Excerpts: 'below approximately two people per square meter, people can generally walk comfortably' (Waseda WIAS); flow breaks down around 2–3 per m² (Still, summarising Fruin). 'Half a square meter' = 1/2 per m², computed.

sentence: Now bring everyone in, and the crowd keeps spreading, street after street, until it settles into a square you could drive across in under an hour.
claim: 8.2 billion people at 2 per m² cover about 4,100 km², a square about 64 km on a side; at 100 km/h that is about 38 minutes across.
source_title: World Population Prospects 2024 (UN DESA Population Division); news.un.org/en/story/2024/07/1151971
note: Computed in calc.py: area_safe_km2 = 4100, side_safe_km = 64.0; 'under an hour' at a highway speed of 100 km/h (a round figure).

sentence: You could squeeze us tighter, but packed twice as close, a crowd starts to move like a fluid, and that's when it turns dangerous.
claim: Standing crowds become dangerous at about 4–5 people per m² (twice 2 per m²), when individuals can no longer control their movement and the crowd behaves like a fluid.
source_title: Crowd-density thresholds (ScienceAlert; also Waseda University WIAS and NPR on crowd safety), summarising Fruin's levels of service and G. K. Still's crowd science
note: Excerpts: the transition to dangerous is 'generally when the crowd density hits about four people for every square metre' (ScienceAlert); static redline 'more than five people per square metre'. 'Twice as close' = 4 per m². The fluid description is the crowd-science framing (Still); the film never shows a crush.

sentence: So we keep the room, and all of humanity still covers just two or three Londons.
claim: At 2 per m², everyone covers about 2.6 times Greater London's 1,572 km².
note: Computed: 4100 / 1,572 = 2.61; said as 'two or three Londons' (the spine shows ≈ 2.6 × Greater London).

sentence: From orbit, you'd struggle to find us.
claim: That area is about 0.003% of Earth's land (148.9 million km²).
source_title: Countries by area (Nations Online): Earth's land 148,940,000 km²
note: Computed: 0.0028%. 'You'd struggle to find us from orbit' is the plain-words version of that fraction (a square 64 km across is visible from orbit, but it is a speck against the land).

sentence: And packed like water, every body would fit in a cube a little shorter than the world's tallest tower.
claim: 8.2 billion bodies at an average of 62 kg and about the density of water make about 0.5 km³: a cube about 800 m on a side, a little shorter than the 828 m Burj Khalifa.
source_title: Walpole et al., 'The weight of nations: an estimation of adult human biomass', BMC Public Health 12, 439 (2012)
note: Computed in calc.py: vol_m3 = 5.08e+08, cube_m = 798 (Burj Khalifa 828 m: Guinness World Records). 62 kg is the world's average ADULT mass (Walpole 2012); children weigh less, so this is an upper bound.

sentence: Nudge how dense we are either way, and that cube barely changes size.
claim: Across the body densities sources give (0.97–1.06 g/cm³), the cube's side changes only from about 783 m to 806 m.
source_title: Do some people not float? (Biology Insights): the body is close to the density of water
note: Computed in calc.py (cube_lo_m, cube_hi_m): the sensitivity line; the card shows the range. Sources for body density are weak (0.97–1.06 across popular science pages); a person should confirm against a physiology text.

sentence: It only feels that way from inside a city.
claim: Everyone alive could stand comfortably in about 4,100 km², about 0.003% of the land: space is not what the world is short of.
source_title: Countries by area (Nations Online): Earth's land 148,940,000 km²
note: The takeaway concerns standing room only: it makes no claim about resources, food or housing (a person should check the wording reads that way).
